human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a pragmatic systems contribution combining neural sequence-to-sequence models for direct SQL generation with interactive learning for rapid semantic parser deployment. The work demonstrates technical competence and provides valuable empirical evidence of deployed systems in practice (live user study with 30 users). However, several core claims rest on incomplete evidence: (1) the 'comparable accuracy' claim is undermined by a 6.8% gap on GEO880 (82.5% vs 89.3%) that is not adequately explained; (2) the crowdsourcing cost/quality advantage is asserted but not empirically validated; (3) the interactive learning effectiveness is demonstrated in simulated experiments with perfect feedback, but real feedback has 6.1–6.3% error rates and the impact is not quantified; (4) the 'minimal domain-specific engineering' claim contradicts substantial engineering (entity identification, schema templates, user interface design). The paper's strongest contribution is the complete end-to-end deployed system with live user validation, which is novel in execution for semantic parsing. The paper is honest about limitations (entity identification errors, database incompleteness, user feedback quality) but does not quantify their impact on core claims. The live experiment is small-scale (30 users, 3 stages, 1 domain) with unclear generalization potential. The paper would be strengthened by: (1) explaining the accuracy gap with prior work (e.g., applying Jia & Liang 2016 data recombination technique); (2) empirically validating crowdsourcing cost/quality claims; (3) quantifying the gap between simulated and real interactive learning; (4) analyzing long-term effects of mislabeled training examples; (5) measuring entity identification accuracy; (6) conducting larger-scale user studies. The paper represents solid incremental progress on an important practical problem, with pragmatic systems value but modest technical novelty. Recommend acceptance with revisions addressing the major methodological gaps identified by reviewers.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes a valuable pragmatic contribution by demonstrating a complete end-to-end semantic parsing system with live user validation. The work is technically sound and honest about limitations. However, several core claims require stronger empirical support: (1) The 'comparable accuracy' claim on GEO880 (82.5% vs 89.3% best prior work) needs explanation. Consider applying the Jia & Liang (2016) data recombination technique to see if it closes the gap, or provide detailed error analysis explaining why direct SQL generation is more difficult. (2) The crowdsourcing cost/quality advantage is a core motivation but lacks empirical validation. Consider conducting a small crowdsourcing study comparing SQL vs logical form annotation cost and quality. (3) The gap between simulated (perfect feedback) and real interactive learning (6.1–6.3% error rates) is not quantified. Conduct simulated experiments with realistic error rates and compare learning curves to perfect feedback condition. (4) Long-term effects of mislabeled training examples are not analyzed. Simulate accumulation of mislabeled data over many iterations and measure performance degradation. (5) Entity identification accuracy is not measured despite being acknowledged as error source. Evaluate TF-IDF matching on benchmark datasets and analyze impact on query correctness. (6) The 'minimal domain-specific engineering' claim contradicts substantial engineering (user interface, entity identification, schema templates). Clarify what 'minimal' means and quantify engineering effort. (7) The live experiment is small-scale (30 users, 3 stages). Consider conducting larger-scale studies with multiple domains to strengthen generalization claims. (8) Add statistical significance testing and confidence intervals to all accuracy estimates. These revisions would significantly strengthen the paper's empirical foundation and clarify the practical advantages of your approach.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper presents a systems-oriented contribution combining neural sequence-to-sequence models for direct SQL generation with an interactive feedback loop for rapid semantic parser deployment. The work demonstrates technical soundness and provides empirical evidence across multiple evaluation modes: benchmark experiments (GEO880, ATIS), simulated interactive learning with ablation studies, and a live three-stage user study with 30 users on academic database search. The core novelty lies in pragmatic systems integration and deployment focus rather than individual technical components. The paper is honest about practical challenges (entity identification errors, database incompleteness, user feedback quality issues with 6.1–6.3% error rates, 22.3% non-executable queries) but does not quantify their impact on core claims.

Strengths:
- Complete end-to-end deployed system with live user validation: The paper demonstrates a fully functional system deployed online with real users, providing empirical evidence of interactive learning in practice. This is novel in execution for semantic parsing and moves beyond typical batch-based evaluation.
- Comprehensive multi-faceted empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across benchmarks (GEO880, ATIS), simulated interactive learning with ablation studies, and live user study. This breadth of evaluation provides evidence from multiple perspectives.
- Honest treatment of limitations and failure modes: The paper transparently reports user feedback error rates (6.1% false positives, 6.3% false negatives), database incompleteness issues, 22.3% non-executable queries, and entity identification errors. This transparency increases credibility and identifies areas for future work.
- Well-motivated architectural choice: Direct SQL generation over intermediate logical forms is clearly motivated by practical advantages (executability, crowdsourceability, wide understanding). The design choice is well-articulated and justified.
- Systematic ablation studies: Table 4 provides clear ablation studies showing the contribution of templates and paraphrasing. Simulated interactive learning experiments (Figure 3) analyze batch size effects on annotation effort (Table 7).
- Pragmatic systems-oriented approach: The paper addresses real deployment challenges (entity identification, user interface design, feedback quality) that are often overlooked in academic semantic parsing work. This systems perspective is valuable for practitioners.
- Resource contribution: Release of SCHOLAR dataset (816 utterances with SQL annotations for academic domain) provides a new resource for the community and demonstrates commitment to reproducibility.

Limitations:
- Accuracy gap on GEO880 not adequately explained: The paper claims 'comparable accuracy' but achieves 82.5% vs 89.3% (Jia & Liang 2016), a 6.8 percentage point gap that is substantial in semantic parsing. The paper attributes this to 'increased complexity' of direct SQL generation but provides no quantitative analysis. The paper notes that Jia & Liang's data recombination technique is 'compatible' but does not apply it, leaving open whether this would close the gap. This undermines the core claim that direct SQL generation achieves comparable accuracy.
- Crowdsourcing cost/quality advantage not empirically validated: The paper asserts that SQL annotation is 'easier and cheaper' than logical form annotation and references skilled-labor crowd markets (UpWork), but provides no empirical comparison of annotation cost, quality, or inter-annotator agreement between SQL and logical forms. This is a core motivation for the approach, yet it lacks validation. The paper mentions this as 'future work' rather than demonstrating it.
- Gap between simulated and real interactive learning not quantified: Simulated interactive learning experiments (Figure 3) assume perfect user feedback, but real feedback has 6.1% false positives and 6.3% false negatives (Table 6). The paper does not quantify how these error rates affect learning curves or whether the gap between simulated and real performance is acceptable. This is critical for assessing whether simulated results predict real-world performance.
- Long-term effects of mislabeled training examples not analyzed: The paper reports user feedback error rates (6.1% false positives, 6.3% false negatives) but does not analyze whether these mislabeled examples degrade model performance over many iterations. The paper acknowledges that 'these queries become incorrectly-labeled examples in the training set that may contribute to the deterioration of model accuracy over time' but provides no analysis of cumulative effects. This is critical for assessing the sustainability of the interactive learning approach.
- Entity identification accuracy not quantified despite acknowledged importance: Entity identification via TF-IDF matching is acknowledged as a source of user feedback errors (line 649) and 22.3% of generated queries do not execute, but entity identification accuracy is not measured. The paper provides no evaluation of TF-IDF matching performance or comparison with alternative entity linking approaches. This is a critical component that directly impacts query correctness.

Open Questions:
- How can the 6.8 percentage point accuracy gap on GEO880 (82.5% vs 89.3% best prior work) be explained or closed? Would applying Jia & Liang (2016)'s data recombination technique close the gap? What types of queries does direct SQL generation fail on that logical form approaches handle well? Is the gap fundamental to SQL generation complexity or due to incomplete implementation?
- What is the empirical evidence that SQL annotation is cheaper and easier to obtain than logical form annotation? How do annotation time, cost, inter-annotator agreement, and error rates compare between SQL and logical forms? Can programmers on UpWork reliably annotate SQL queries at scale?
- How do user feedback error rates (6.1% false positives, 6.3% false negatives) affect learning curves in interactive learning? What is the cumulative effect of mislabeled examples over many iterations? At what error rate would feedback quality become insufficient for model improvement? How do error rates in this paper compare to other interactive learning systems?
- What is the entity identification accuracy of TF-IDF matching on benchmark datasets and the live experiment? How much of the 22.3% non-executable query rate is due to entity identification errors vs other factors? How does TF-IDF matching compare to other entity linking approaches?
- Is the improvement in interactive learning due to the feedback loop (selective annotation based on model predictions) or simply due to accumulating more labeled data? What would be the learning curve if examples were randomly sampled instead of selectively annotated based on model predictions?

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about limitations and failure modes (entity identification errors, database incompleteness, user feedback quality issues, 22.3% non-executable queries), which increases credibility. The paper acknowledges that Jia & Liang (2016) data recombination technique is 'compatible' with the model but does not apply it, leaving open whether this would close the accuracy gap. The paper transparently reports that templates do not improve fully supervised performance on GEO880, which contradicts claims of importance for bootstrapping; this inconsistency is not adequately explained. The paper does not discuss computational cost of interactive learning (model training time, crowdsourcing overhead, user interface maintenance) or potential privacy concerns with releasing academic database queries in the SCHOLAR dataset. The paper's framing of 'rapid deployment' (three days) could be clearer about what is included in this timeline. The paper does not provide code or implementation details beyond algorithm pseudocode, limiting reproducibility.

Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Given this rep- resentation, we conceptualize semantic pars- ing as a graph matching problem. Our model converts sentences to semantic graphs using CCG and subsequently grounds them to Free- base guided by denotations as a form of weak supervision. For example, the feature rep- resentation in Chen and Manning (2014) is a con- catenation of 18 word vectors, 18 POS vectors and 12 dependency-label vectors.3 The above works tackle the effort in hand-crafting effective feature combinations. A different line of work attacks the feature-engineering problem by suggesting novel neural-network architectures for encoding the parser state, including intermediately- built subtrees, as vectors which are then fed to non- linear classiﬁers. Titov and Henderson encode the parser state using incremental sigmoid-belief net- works (2007). In the work of Dyer et al. (2015), the entire stack and buffer of a transition-based parser are encoded as a stack-LSTMs, where each stack el- ement is itself based on a compositional represen- tation of parse trees. Le and Zuidema (2014) en- code each tree node as two compositional represen- tations capturing the inside and outside structures around the node, and feed the representations into a reranker. A similar reranking approach, this time based on convolutional neural networks, is taken by Zhu et al. (2015). Finally, in Kiperwasser and Gold- berg (2016) we present an Easy-First parser based on a novel hierarchical-LSTM tree encoding.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.

Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

While the move to neural-network classi- ﬁers alleviates the need for hand-crafting feature- combinations, the need to carefully deﬁne a set of core features remain. For example, the feature rep- resentation in Chen and Manning (2014) is a con- catenation of 18 word vectors, 18 POS vectors and 12 dependency-label vectors.3 The above works tackle the effort in hand-crafting effective feature combinations. A different line of work attacks the feature-engineering problem by suggesting novel neural-network architectures for encoding the parser state, including intermediately- built subtrees, as vectors which are then fed to non- linear classiﬁers. Titov and Henderson encode the parser state using incremental sigmoid-belief net- works (2007). In the work of Dyer et al. (2015), the entire stack and buffer of a transition-based parser are encoded as a stack-LSTMs, where each stack el- ement is itself based on a compositional represen- tation of parse trees. Le and Zuidema (2014) en- code each tree node as two compositional represen- tations capturing the inside and outside structures around the node, and feed the representations into a reranker. A similar reranking approach, this time based on convolutional neural networks, is taken by Zhu et al. (2015). Finally, in Kiperwasser and Gold- berg (2016) we present an Easy-First parser based on a novel hierarchical-LSTM tree encoding.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

(2011) used a graphical model semantics rep- resentation to learn from instructions paired with demonstrations. In contrast, we model signiﬁcantly more complex linguistic phenomena than these ap- proaches, as required for the navigation domain. Other research has adopted expressive meaning representations, with differing learning approaches. Matuszek et al. (2010, 2012) describe supervised al- gorithms that learn semantic parsers for navigation instructions. Chen and Mooney (2011), Chen (2012) and Kim and Mooney (2012) present state-of-the- art algorithms for the navigation task, by training a supervised semantic parser from automatically in- duced labels. Our work differs in the use of joint learning and inference approaches. Supervised approaches for learning semantic parsers have received signiﬁcant attention, e.g. Kate and Mooney (2006), Wong and Mooney (2007), Muresan (2011) and Kwiatkowski et al. (2010, 2012). The algorithms we develop in this pa- per combine ideas from previous supervised CCG learning work (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005, 2007; Kwiatkowski et al., 2011), as we describe in Sec- tion 4. top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.title: Weakly Supervised Learning of Semantic Parsers for Mapping Instructions to Actions
top_documents.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: (2010) extended their RL ap- proach to model high-level instructions, which cor- respond to implicit actions in our domain. Wei et al. (2009) and Kollar et al. (2010) used shallow linguis- tic representations for instructions. Recently, Tellex 50 Downloaded from http://www.mitpressjournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1162/tacl_a_00209 by guest on 20 July 2026 et al. (2011) used a graphical model semantics rep- resentation to learn from instructions paired with demonstrations. In contrast, we model signiﬁcantly more complex linguistic phenomena than these ap- proaches, as required for the navigation domain. Other research has adopted expressive meaning representations, with differing learning approaches. Matuszek et al. (2010, 2012) describe supervised al- gorithms that learn semantic parsers for navigation instructions. Chen and Mooney (2011), Chen (2012) and Kim and Mooney (2012) present state-of-the- art algorithms for the navigation task, by training a supervised semantic parser from automatically in- duced labels. Our work differs in the use of joint learning and inference approaches. Supervised approaches for learning semantic parsers have received signiﬁcant attention, e.g. Kate and Mooney (2006), Wong and Mooney (2007), Muresan (2011) and Kwiatkowski et al. (2010, 2012). The algorithms we develop in this pa- per combine ideas from previous supervised CCG learning work (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005, 2007; Kwiatkowski et al., 2011), as we describe in Sec- tion 4. Recently, various alternative forms of su- pervision were introduced.

top_documents.title: Modelling and Optimizing on Syntactic N-Grams for Statistical Machine Translation
top_documents.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: other parsing models that have been used for language modelling, such as lexicalized PCFGs (Charniak, 2001; Collins, 2003; Charniak et al., 2003), or struc- tured language models (Chelba and Jelinek, 2000); previous efforts to include them in the translation process failed to improve translation performance (Och et al., 2004; Post and Gildea, 2008). Differ- ences in our work that could explain why we see im- provements include the use of Neural Networks for training the model on the automatically parsed train- ing text, instead of re-using existing parser mod- els, which could be seen as a form of self-training (McClosky et al., 2006), and the integration of the language model into the decoder instead of n-best reranking. Also, there are major differences in the parsing models themselves. For instance, note that the structured LM by Chelba and Jelinek (2000) uses a binary branching structure, and that complex label sets would be required to encode subcategorisation frames in binary trees (Hockenmaier and Steedman, 2002). Our neural network is a standard feed-forward neural network as introduced by Bengio et al. (2003). Recently, recursive neural networks have been proposed for syntactic parsing (Socher et al., 2010; Le and Zuidema, 2014). The recursive na- ture of such models allows for the encoding of more context; for an efﬁcient integration into the dynamic programming search

Section: ✅ TASK 2. Assignment check
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, policy_screen
Content: n doubt, consider the scope described in ARR CFP and any relevant conferences (e.g. for October 2024 cycle the NAACL CFP specifies the special theme “NLP in a Multicultural World”. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

Section: 🆕 4. Check for common problems in NLP papers
Codes: M1, G2
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor
Content: As a counter to common problems with reviews, there are also common problems with NLP papers. We do ask you to watch out for these and point them out when you see them. Above all else, published research should at least be technically sound and appropriately scoped. As with the above reviewer issues, it’s a case-by-case evaluation: some things in the list below may be appropriate in a given context, given that they are sufficiently motivated. We provide codes for different types of issues (e.g. M1, G2…) that can be referenced in discussions.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
